summary.7-10: A stranger helps a man everyone else walked past.
summary.11-14: Jesus answers 'who is my neighbour?' with a story.
summary.15-18: A parable that dismantles the question it was asked.

7-10: A man was walking along a lonely road when robbers attacked him and left him hurt.
Two religious men walked past on the other side. Then a man from Samaria came along — someone people said was an enemy.
He stopped. He cleaned the man's cuts, put him on his own donkey, took him to an inn and paid for him to be looked after. Jesus said: be like him.
11-14: A lawyer asked Jesus how to inherit eternal life, then — 'wanting to justify himself' — asked who counted as his neighbour. Jesus told a story instead of giving a definition.
A man is robbed and left half dead on the road down to Jericho. A priest sees him and crosses over. A Levite does the same. Both were religious professionals.

Then a Samaritan — from a people Jews despised and avoided — stops, treats the wounds, puts the man on his own animal, pays for his care and promises to cover any extra. Jesus turns the lawyer's question round: not 'who is my neighbour?' but 'which of these was a neighbour?'
15-18: The lawyer's question is a boundary question: he wants to know where the obligation stops. Jesus refuses to answer it and replaces it with a different one.

The parable's shock is not that the priest and Levite were villains — a corpse would have made them ritually unclean, and their caution was defensible. The shock is that the person who acts is a Samaritan, from a group with whom Jews shared a bitter, centuries-old religious quarrel.

The closing exchange is precise. Jesus asks which man 'became a neighbour', and the lawyer cannot even say the word Samaritan; he says 'the one who showed mercy'. The question of who deserves my love has been replaced with the question of what kind of person I am becoming.

whatHappened.7-10: A man from Samaria helped a hurt stranger when nobody else would.
whatHappened.11-14: Two religious men walked past a wounded man; a despised foreigner stopped and paid for his care.
whatHappened.15-18: Jesus answers a boundary question with a story that makes the hated outsider the moral example.

whatItTeaches.7-10: Being a good neighbour means helping whoever needs you.
whatItTeaches.11-14: Jesus refuses to let 'neighbour' be a category you can narrow. He turns it into something you become.
whatItTeaches.15-18: The parable converts an ethical question about obligation into a question about identity and mercy.

thinkAboutIt.7-10: Who could you help this week?
thinkAboutIt.11-14: Have you ever walked past someone because helping was inconvenient?
thinkAboutIt.15-18: The lawyer wanted a boundary. Where are you quietly maintaining one?

pray.7-10: Jesus, help me notice people who need help, and actually help them.
pray.11-14: Jesus, make me the kind of person who stops, even when stopping costs something.
pray.15-18: Jesus, take away my instinct to define the limits of who I owe love to.

prompt.7-10: Who stopped to help the hurt man?
prompt.15-18: Why is the helper's identity the point of the parable?

explain.7-10: A man from Samaria — someone people thought of as an enemy.
explain.11-14: A Samaritan, from a group Jews despised and avoided.
explain.15-18: Because the moral exemplar is drawn from the group the audience most despised, which is what breaks the boundary question.
